sections.overview: The Bohemian Waxwing is a crested, starling-sized passerine of northern Eurasia and North America. It is one of three waxwing species, alongside the Cedar Waxwing and the more easterly Japanese Waxwing.
sections.identification: Its gray-brown plumage, chestnut face, pointed crest, yellow tail tip and red wax-like feather tips distinguish it from the browner, yellow-bellied Cedar Waxwing. The two species share a sleek crest and flocking habits.
sections.habitat: It breeds in northern coniferous and mixed forests, then wanders widely wherever fruit crops are available. In towns and suburbs, fruiting trees can attract winter flocks.
sections.diet: Berries and other fruits dominate its nonbreeding diet, while flying insects become important during the breeding season. Rowan, juniper and other persistent fruits can draw large flocks when northern food supplies fail.
sections.behavior: Flocks move nomadically in search of fruit, and winter numbers south of the breeding range vary greatly between years. These irregular irruptions track changes in food availability.
sections.reproduction: It nests in northern woodland and breeds later than many passerines, when summer food is abundant. A clutch usually numbers four to six eggs, and both parents feed the nestlings.
sections.ecology: By eating fruit and spreading seeds, it helps disperse plants across its wide seasonal range. Its dependence on fruit crops links movements to annual variation in woodland food.
sections.conservation: It remains widespread, but Cornell Lab reports a steep long-term decline in North America. Conservation outlook should be interpreted regionally because trends vary across its range.
